title: Breaking And Entering: Cat Power Reflects On Bob Dylan’s Influence
summary: Ahead of her tour, Cat Power Sings Dylan, acclaimed American singer-songwriter Cat Power talks in retrospect about her lifelong admiration of Bob Dylan. She chats to Simon and Lauren about how growing up listening to Bob Dylan’s music fostered her songwriting style and how songs like ‘Mr Tambourine Man’ introduced to her a blend of punk's raw lyricism with softer melodies.
transcript:
Chan Marshall, who performs as Cat Power, spoke with Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler about her lifelong relationship with Bob Dylan's music, ahead of her Cat Power Sings Dylan performance at Festival Hall in Melbourne. The conversation was broadcast on Triple R on 20 February 2025. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: You Are Free, the sixth studio album by Cat Power, aka Chan Marshall, came out this week 22 years ago, and it's always a good time to revisit that extraordinary record. More recently, Cat Power has spent a lot of time touring not her own music, but Bob Dylan's 1966 Royal Albert Hall concert, the show that famously marked Dylan's controversial shift to electric. For her, it connects directly back to her earliest memories of Dylan's music: watching how adults would argue about his songs at parties in Georgia in the 1970s. She has said many times that she never had a favourite artist apart from Bob Dylan. Here she begins by describing her first encounter with him, when he was an enigma before he became an influence.

Chan: I met my mum and my dad when I was five. All the people that came with them when I met them were musicians. I noticed the way they would act when a Bob Dylan song came on at a party, or at the house, or wherever we were. I noticed how people would behave differently. His songs reminded me somewhat of, it was familiar in the way of a fable.

What made me notice him was the way the adults behaved when his music came on. They would talk about him as if he'd done something wrong, or he was being criticised. I wasn't sure. I didn't understand why they were playing his music if they didn't like the guy, or why there were so many opinions about this person. Because I didn't understand what a good voice was or what a good lyric was. I didn't understand the context of critiquing anything. I learned that people had a lot to say about Bob, and that introduced me to my own curiosity.

I became curious about him because when it was Jimi Hendrix, or David Bowie, you know, Ziggy Stardust, there was a lot of oohing and aahing. There wasn't any kind of discrepancy or caution. I think I gravitated to his songs because I felt like they were casting him as an underdog in some kind of way. I didn't understand until I was older that it was just schools of thought, basically. I think some people preferred the rock and roll antics to the critical-thinking poetry kind of thing, the beat sort of thing he was doing.

Lauren: What was the first Dylan song or lyric that really spoke to you?

Chan: I think 'Mr Tambourine Man'. Because, again, I've never been tested for autism. I'm just saying this. Now we have words like neurotypical and neurodivergent. But I know that as a little girl, I really lived in songs, and I know a lot of people that love music felt that too. I really just felt whole in them. I could escape. It was very visual for me, colourful, blah, blah, blah.

The only reason I'm saying that is because songs play a really big, important — they're almost like a family member to me. I haven't met very many people who have that sort of neurological, psychological thing with music. I think the first one for me was 'Mr Tambourine Man'. I felt like it was, and still is, the most transcendental. It feels like a photograph of a dream, or a fairy tale. These fairy tales we write, or that have been written, are always going to end up great. The fairy tale is going to work out.

That's the thing about 'Mr Tambourine Man': there's some hardship there, but you can almost taste it. It feels really sweet and believable, even though it's so preposterous. It's like he's screaming from the earth, 'Get me out of here,' you know what I mean?

Simon: That's beautifully put. There's some magic in it, for sure.

Chan: I feel like Bob has that same jester-ish thing of, the king can't be told the truth or he'll get his head cut off. So you want the truth in a riddle, you want it in a joke, a song, a dance. I've always felt like Bob has had that sort of magician way about his lyrics, to charm you into thinking properly about stuff, which is really a gift.

Lauren: It's a great cover that you do of 'Mr Tambourine Man'. We've spoken in the past about your view of covers as a form of musical conversation, and you've said that covering other people's songs can be like medicine for you. Can you describe the conversation you've had with Dylan through covering his music, and how his music has been like medicine for you?

Chan: Oh man. When I was in junior high, there was an English teacher who was also the basketball coach, and that happened very frequently. My science teacher was the gym teacher. But anyway, I wanted to do a punk rock song, but I thought, I can't go too far outside of the conservatism. So I thought, well, I'll do this Bob Dylan song, because nobody knows this song.

I thought if I did my report, if I spoke these words out to the class, it would be something different that maybe they would be interested in. I was about 12 years old. I chose that song because of how I saw the caste system in the South. If you're poor, you're nothing. Doesn't matter your colour, your ethnicity, nothing. If you're poor, you're nothing. Teachers don't like you. No one likes you. It was all about being poor.

Everybody else was doing major pop songs from the time; MTV was huge. I feel like that's the first time I ever covered Bob Dylan, bringing his lyrics to a group of people who never would have wanted to listen to that kind of music. But obviously, when I started playing guitar and singing songs professionally, choosing to sing for 40 bucks a night and free food instead of working five jobs a week to pay my rent, I really enjoyed playing different covers. I just thought, oh well, these are some of the songs I know. No one's going to like the songs I'm going to sing. My songs are about committing suicide and fighting Satan and things that no one wants to hear about.

But if I sing this beautiful Bob Dylan song, 'Moonshiner': to this day, I rarely hear that recording, but if you played it for me right now, it would suspend time for me. I would be lost in whatever vortex he created. I do believe in songs being medicine, a prescription to sort of stop time, to heal something that's a part of us all. I don't know, something transcendental again. He's been around since I was little. Bob's still kicking around on earth and still recording great records. I think I'll always be covering Bob's songs, I'm guessing.

Simon: It's beautiful to hear you talk about that connection with his music. To continue the idea of your covers as conversation, there's a balance between staying true to the original and introducing your own narrative shift or style. One example is 'She Belongs to Me', where you move the perspective of the narrator. Could you tell us about those creative choices, and how you find a place within the songs?

Chan: Well, I think just because I happen to be born a female and am cis, I am straight and a woman, singing from a personal perspective about 'she' does give a different angle to the audience member and the listener.

For myself, right now, I feel choked up thinking about the power that we as women have, to have survived this crazy ride of a life. For all of us that are still standing, still getting through the quiet part, getting through the loud part, having to be louder than we want to be to get our point across to deaf ears our whole life. Singing this song, it really is so enormous, how I feel. The room is huge with this feminine energy, this divine creative energy.

When I hear Dylan singing, for example, 'To Ramona' — I don't know if you know that song — when he's singing to Ramona, as a teenage girl that brought me to my knees. To have a song explicitly in honour of a female was so empowering for me as a young girl. I've never heard no song by no man that so eloquently and elegantly, with a ton of grace, respectfully donates art to womanhood. That's what I feel 'She Belongs to Me' is, in a similar vein.

To sing it as a woman in front of people, in front of young girls, in front of even elderly men who maybe have never had the epiphany of what it could be like for their daughter or granddaughter or wife or mother to have experienced the things that we've repeatedly asked someone to listen to, and just to be on our team. I really love singing that song. Sometimes it's hard, because as a woman, sometimes you do feel very alone. There are occasions, singing that song, when I do feel very alone.

I just hope that everybody knows, hey man, I didn't write this song, but I feel really powerful singing it. I hope that the women that receive it and the men that receive it, non-binary, everybody that receives it, understand how I feel when I'm singing. I feel like we are all capable of powerful love and creative, positive nature. I love that song. I love that he wrote that song. It's beautiful.

Lauren: Chan, when we spoke to you back in 2018, around the release of Wanderer, when you came into Triple R, we talked about archetypes like the wanderer, and with that album you were going back to the archetype of the teller of the tale, which Dylan represents. Is this recording and this tour also a way of honouring that archetype? Is that how you see it?

Chan: Well, it's interesting you brought that up. Back then, in 2018, I had definitely struggled through getting dropped by my label, being a single mum, and then suddenly, oh well, now I'm dropped from my label. There were a lot of things that didn't occur to me at the time. My son's nine years old now; he's going to be ten in April. Having all that time to ruminate: wow, I really did get dropped from a label when I became a mother.

When you're going through certain strifes in life, you don't have time to sort of — you've got to pack up and run. You've got to do your best in that moment. I think as we get older, we get better, and we get calmer, we get wiser. That's just how I feel. We take better care of ourselves. We know ourselves better.

Being the teller of the tale: I think all my records have always kind of been on my own. I know I've had musical support from great musicians, and I've been very lucky in that way. But I have always been doing these songs as somebody who definitely respects the singer of the song. That's sometimes what makes a favourite song a favourite song for me. The same song can be sung by ten different people. You both, and anyone listening, will know what I'm talking about. You can have one song sung by a lot of people, but there's always going to be that artist, like Dylan, Billie Holiday, Willie Nelson, Nina Simone, where the singer becomes the song. 'I love that song. Oh, Patsy Cline's version.'

I think that's what Bob does, even with his own material. You love that sort of magic when someone does a cover: 'Oh wow, this is so different, and my heart is expanding because of the way this person's vibrato sounds. It's so different, and it's moving me to tears and opening my soul.' That's just the singer, right? And Bob has both. You can hear his lyrics and his voice. It's his truth: the teller, the tale. Every time I hear Bob singing, it just sounds like the truth. I'm not saying I'm Bob Dylan or Billie Holiday, but me singing Bob Dylan's songs is an homage to that feeling of having deep love for the teller of the tale, the singer of the song, even though these happen to be his songs.

Simon: It's also interesting to look at songs as moments in time, with recordings capturing a particular spark or electricity at a moment in history. That relates to the recordings you've made of the Royal Albert Hall concert, which in a way honour a legendary performance by Bob Dylan, but also deepen the story yet again, adding layers to its history and meaning.

Chan: Just to move it on down the line. The world is getting more f'd up every moment. It's a way, like a conveyor belt: okay, let's do this. Like you're saying, moments in time, a spark. Who knows, maybe someone down the line will, like this movie, the dang movie that just came out with Timothée Chalamet, you know what I'm saying?

Lauren: Have you seen it yet?

Chan: I haven't. I'm a real snob about movie theatres. I need to sit in a movie theatre, and I have my son. We could talk about this at length, but he doesn't want to see the movie, because I've been on tour with Bob Dylan's songs. He's like, 'Oh, you want me to sit in a movie and watch a movie about Bob, when you've been away from me for a year? No, I don't want to see the movie.' So I haven't had a moment to actually go and see it. But I'm going to see it eventually, of course.

But you know what I'm saying? What the fuck did I do the record for? What did I do the tour for, if it's already a thing? You know what I mean? I don't know if I wasted my time.

Simon: Not at all.

Chan: But you see what I'm saying?

Simon: From one perspective, it's a celebration of the recordings, and it's, as you say —

Chan: I think that he went electric because we've got to wake everybody up: the time is happening, things are changing. Maybe I'm just putting my ideas onto that moment in time, but it was crazy, just like it is right now, the things going on in America. That's why I wanted to do that concert, because things were so messed up at the time. Abortion was deemed illegal. There was so much going on in America when I was like, 'Do it, let's just go, let's just do this. Let's just go do it.'

Because I thought, I've tried, I'm not very good academically. I wish I could be President of the United States. It ain't going to happen in my lifetime. I tried doing well in high school; it didn't work out. I have ADHD. I'm not really good with concentrating. I'm just not a good student. Let me just do these songs. Maybe it'll trigger people's memory of the past. Maybe they'll remember. It's like a testament. Bob's still alive, running around, making great work still.

I see this movie coming out and it's a direct hit. It's got amazing ratings. Timothée Chalamet just came out with the soundtrack of all the songs he recorded live. So in a way, I feel like I didn't waste my time. I love Bob so much, and I definitely would have done this no matter what. But I worked so hard on the year of touring. It's my job. That's how I earn a living, touring. I guess we all second-guess ourselves, and that's human nature. I just hope that it wasn't for nothing.

With the state the world is in, I'm not saying putting out a record of when Bob Dylan went electric is going to change the world. But I just don't know what to do, as an artist. When I get home from this Australian thing, I've already been recording; I've already started my next record. I guess that's what we just have to keep doing.
